pass_a_gloss: [...] having been revealed, those things were among praises for many. Thus also it is written about both Zechariah and Elizabeth: And there was in the days of Herod the king of Judaea a certain priest, Zechariah by name, from the daily course of Abijah, and his wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, going in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. According to this manner, I think, the holy prophets themselves too lived through. And indeed also the divine Paul, although saying openly that he became blameless according to the righteousness in law: But what was gain to me? These things, he says, I have considered loss because of Christ. So before the sojourn of the Saviour of us all, Christ, some well esteemed for the glories according to law were both manly and youthful. But after his appearing, and the gospel proclamation, the things in law have ceased, the shadow has moved over toward truth, and the worship in spirit and true has been brought in. So God does not rejoice over the young men of the Jews, that is, those still being manly through choosing to live lawfully. And not accepted are the sacrifices through bloods, and circumcision of flesh, teachings of washings, and idlenesses of Sabbaths. And we have been taught, as I said, the way of the way of life pleasing to God. Cast off then, and very fittingly, after the ending of the shadow, are the young men according to it; and far from being pitied orphans and widows. And orphans he says those as it were needing the spiritual upbringing, and the tutoring from teachers. And widows likewise we say are souls that have come into want of being able to bear fruit, because of not having the sower and supplier for them of all the good lessons. And that we will find those from Israel without share of true instruction, because of the drunken outrage toward Christ, no one would praise. For their eyes were darkened so as not to see, according to the voice of the one singing psalms. And their backs were bent together. And this continually, so as not to be able to see the things above, but as it were stooping, to be fixed upon the earthly things. And they will suffer this, he says, not in vain; but because all have become lawless and wicked, and every mouth speaks lawless things. For how not lawless, and full of all wickedness, those who were eager to put around with death the one calling to life, the one who did not know sin, although the law saying clearly: Innocent and righteous you will not kill? How has not every tongue of the Jews spoken unjust things? For they had cried down Christ to Pilate, saying: Away, away, crucify him. And, Unless [you] kill this [man] [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: …revealed, those things were held in high praise. So it is also written of Zechariah and Elizabeth: “In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1:5-6). In this way, I think, the holy prophets themselves also lived. And indeed the inspired Paul, though he says openly that he had been “blameless as to the righteousness in the Law” (Philippians 3:6), says: “But whatever was gain to me, these things I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ” (Philippians 3:7).

So before the coming of Christ, the Savior of us all, some who were well esteemed for the glories of the Law were strong and in the vigor of youth. But after His appearing and the preaching of the Gospel, the things of the Law have ceased, the shadow has passed over into the truth, and the worship that is in spirit and in truth has been brought in (John 4:23). God therefore does not rejoice over the young men of the Jews (Isaiah 9:17), that is, over those who still show their strength by choosing to live according to the Law. The sacrifices offered through blood are not accepted, nor circumcision of the flesh, nor teachings about washings, nor the idleness of the Sabbaths. But we have been taught, as I said, the way of the life that pleases God.

So, quite rightly, once the shadow came to an end, the young men who live by it are cast off, and the orphans and widows are far from being pitied (Isaiah 9:17). By orphans he means those who, as it were, lack spiritual upbringing and the guidance that comes from teachers. Likewise we say that the widows are souls that have come to lack the power to bear fruit, because they do not have the one who sows and supplies for them all good teachings.

No one would praise the state in which we shall find the people of Israel: without any share in true instruction because of their drunken outrage against Christ. For “their eyes were darkened so that they could not see,” as the psalmist says, and “their backs were bent” (Psalm 69:23), and this “continually,” so that they cannot look at the things above but, as if stooped over, are fixed on earthly things.

They will suffer this, he says, not without cause, but because “all have become lawless and wicked, and every mouth speaks lawless things” (Isaiah 9:17). For how are they not lawless and full of every wickedness, who strove to bring death upon the One who calls them to life, the One who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), although the Law says plainly, “You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous” (Exodus 23:7)? How has not every tongue of the Jews spoken unjust things? For they cried out against Christ to Pilate, saying, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” (John 19:15). And, “Unless you kill this man…”

choices.english: You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous
choices.why: Exodus 23:7 is a prohibition; it is not a question 'will you not kill?'.
rejected: Will you not kill the innocent and the just?

choices.why: πείσονται is from πάσχω, 'they will suffer', not from πείθω.
Cyril's figurative reading of the orphans of Isaiah 9:17.
ἀργία, rest from work; one of the shadows that have ceased.
παροινία, behaviour like a drunkard's; Cyril's charge, translated as written.
